# Dantabhūmi Sutta (MN 125 (PTS MN iii 128))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dantabhūmi Sutta* ("The Level of the Tamed", MN 125 / PTS MN iii 128) is the 125th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens when Prince Jayasena visits the novice Aciravata to ask whether an ardent, undistracted, and resolute monk can attain one-pointedness of mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*) [Norman 1983; Shulman 2014]. When Aciravata's explanation fails to convince the prince—who maintains that someone immersed in sensual pleasures cannot realize such peace—the novice reports the exchange to the Buddha [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Hazra 1994]. The Buddha explains that Prince Jayasena, accustomed to the pleasures of worldly life, could not see what is known only through renunciation, and shows how Aciravata could have answered by employing similes drawn from the training and taming of wild elephants, a domain with which the prince was familiar [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2003].

The sutta sets forth a standard gradual training scheme (*sīla*, *samādhi*, *paññā*, and *vimutti*) comparable to discourses such as MN 27 and MN 51 [Shonin et al. 2015]. In its presentation of meditation, the practice of the four *satipaṭṭhāna*s is placed after the abandonment of the hindrances and functions as an intermediate step leading directly into *jhāna* [Sujato 2012; Anālayo 2003]. Here the meditator is instructed to contemplate the body, feelings, mind, and mind-objects while deliberately refraining from thoughts connected with the body or sensual desire (*mā ca kāmūpasaṁhitaṁ vitakkaṁ vitakkesi* / *kāyūpasaṁhitaṁ*) [Sujato 2012; Polak 2011].

A full parallel to the sutta is preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 198) [SuttaCentral], which has been studied and translated into English by Bhikkhu Anālayo [Bibliogr. Transl. 2015; Shulman 2014]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus aligns MN 125 with MĀ (ZH_T01_0026_052, agreeing with MĀ 198), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and several Tibetan texts including the *Vinayavastu* and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, substantial formulaic passages of the gradual training (§13–14) are shared with discourses such as the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), *Subha Sutta* (DN 10), AN 4.198, MN 27, MN 51, and MN 101 [DharmaNexus]. The sutta's distinctive phrasing on thought-free *satipaṭṭhāna* also appears adapted in the Mahāyāna *Pratyutpannabuddhasammukhāvasthitasamādhi Sūtra* [Sujato 2012].
